prompt: Governments have limited budgets for health care. Some people believe that public money should always be spent on preventing illness rather than on treating it. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
essay:
Every health system spends more than it has, so the choice between preventing illness and treating it is a real one rather than a theoretical exercise. I agree that prevention deserves a far larger share than it usually receives, but the word 'always' in this claim is what I would reject.

The economic argument for prevention is strong and well established. Vaccination, screening programmes and measures that reduce smoking cost a fraction of what it costs to treat the conditions they avert, and they go on delivering that saving for decades. Prevention also reaches people who would otherwise not appear at a hospital until their illness was advanced, which is the point at which treatment is least effective and most expensive. A system that funds only treatment is in effect waiting for problems it could have avoided and then paying the higher price for them.

The difficulty is that prevention and treatment are not interchangeable claims on the same budget. A person who is already ill cannot be helped by a campaign, and a government that redirected all its funding towards prevention would be abandoning identifiable people in order to benefit statistical ones. Prevention is also uncertain at the level of the individual: a screening programme saves lives without anyone being able to say whose. The visible patient tends to win that argument, and it is not obvious that they should lose it.

My view is that the balance should shift substantially towards prevention but can never become absolute. A sensible rule would protect treatment for those already ill and direct new money towards prevention, which is where each additional pound buys the most health. Existing services would be protected and the shift would happen at the margin.
title: Whether prevention should always come before treatment
